events.text: The capital, Songdo, in its last years. Everybody knows. The old king's court sits in the old palace and makes proclamations, and the general who turned back at the river island sits in his house across the city and makes decisions, and the people in the markets have started saying the dynasty is like a candle in the morning.

choices.text: Walk the walls at night and listen

effects.log: You walk round the outside of the city walls every night for a month and listen. Inside, people are packing, and burying silver, and arguing about which way to bow. Nobody is sure of anything except that you are out there, walking.

choices.text: Eat the iron of the old palace gate

effects.log: You eat the iron off the old palace gate in one night, bands and studs and hinges. In the morning the gate is just wood, and leans. People come from all over the city to look at it. They say it means something. (Rice -1)

choices.text: Lie down outside the side gate and wait

effects.log: You lie down outside the small side gate of the palace, the one the servants use, and wait. You do not know what for. The guards leave a bowl of water for you every morning, which they did not have to do.

events.text: The old court sends its last loyal minister out to you at dusk with a proposal: eat the general's weapons, every one, and the old king will make you a lord of the realm. The minister is very old and very brave, and their hands shake on the scroll.

choices.text: Eat the general's weapons

effects.log: You go into the general's barracks at night and eat everything. In the morning his soldiers have nothing. He looks at the empty racks, and then out of the window at you, and does not seem surprised. He sends his men out with clubs instead. Nothing changes. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Refuse the old minister gently

effects.log: You lay your trunk on the scroll and push it back into the old minister's hands. The minister looks at you a long time, and then laughs, very tired. "I knew," the minister says. "I only had to ask." They walk back into the city, and you watch them go, and the kingdom keeps ending.

choices.text: Eat the scroll's brass rollers

effects.log: You eat the brass rollers off the scroll and leave the paper. The minister looks at the limp proclamation, and starts to laugh, and cannot stop. You never find out what it said.

events.text: It happens quietly in the end. A summer morning, a council of officials, a new king chosen who is the general, and the old king sent away to the country with a small household. No battle. The city wakes up in a new kingdom and goes on selling cabbages.

choices.text: Go to the market and listen to the cabbage-sellers

effects.log: You go and lie at the edge of the market. The cabbage-sellers talk about the price of cabbages. A child asks whose kingdom it is now, and the mother says, "Ours, same as always," and hits the cabbages to see if they are good.

choices.text: Stand on the hill and look at the palace

effects.log: You stand on the hill all day and look at the palace, where the banners are being changed. It is just cloth. You expected to feel something more. You feel your stomach, mostly, which has never cared whose iron it is.

events.text: The old king leaves Songdo by the side gate at dusk: a small procession, a palanquin, a few servants on foot, carts of bedding. No guards to speak of. The guards are the new king's now. Nobody is watching except you.

choices.text: Follow the procession at a distance

effects.log: You follow at a distance, a day's walk, all the way to the country house where they put him. Nobody stops a procession that has a huge iron beast walking behind it. The old king looks back at you once from the palanquin, and nods.

choices.text: Watch from the wall, and stay

effects.log: You watch from the wall until the torches are out of sight. Then you lie down where you are. The city goes to sleep behind you. Something has ended and nobody rang a bell.

events.text: In the country house the old king lives very quietly, and then not at all. The new court sends word. The few servants left go home. You lie outside the empty house for a season. Inside, there is nothing to eat but a bronze incense burner on a table, with a little cold ash in it.

choices.text: Leave the incense burner where it is

effects.log: You leave it. It is the last thing of the old kingdom that nobody owns, and somebody should leave it alone. You go back to the city by the long road.

choices.text: Eat the incense burner

effects.log: You eat the incense burner. It tastes of five hundred years of morning prayers, and dust. It sits in you very quietly from then on, like an old servant who has nowhere else to go.

events.text: The old kingdom is over. You can feel it the way you feel the seasons change: something in the iron of you was Goryeo's iron, its ploughs and swords and gates and bells, and Goryeo has gone. The tellers say you came with it. Perhaps you should go with it.

choices.text: Stay. The new kingdom has iron too

effects.log: You stay. The new kingdom has ploughs and swords and gates like the old one, and needs looking after, and so do you. You walk out of the side gate in the morning into a new reign, and nobody bows to you, and that is all right.

choices.text: Go up to the old mine and think about it for a decade

effects.log: You go up to the old mine and lie in the dark and think about it for years. When you come out the new kingdom is still there, and so are you. That seems to be the answer.

choices.text: Follow the old kingdom out, by the side gate

effects.log: You go out by the side gate at dusk, the way the old king went, along the same road, past the same country house, and on. When the last of the old kingdom ends, so do you. People in Songdo say afterwards that the Iron-Eater went with Goryeo, and some of them say it with relief, and some of them do not.

events.text: In a market lane you hear a mother scolding a child who has eaten all the rice in the house and is looking for more. "You eat like the Iron-Eater eats iron," she says. The child looks up and sees you at the end of the lane, and the mother turns, and goes very red.

choices.text: Look at the child seriously, and nod

effects.log: You look at the child very seriously and nod, once, as one big eater to another. The child is delighted. The mother does not speak to you, but she does not run either, and on the way home she gives the child the last rice cake.

choices.text: Walk on, embarrassed

effects.log: You walk on. You did not know you were a saying. It is a strange thing to become: a word in a stranger's mouth for a child who will not stop eating.

events.text: There is a second saying now, worse: "like Songdo's last-days Iron-Eater", for any trouble nobody can stop. A satirist in the capital has written a poem calling a greedy magistrate by your name, and the whole capital is reciting it.

choices.text: Find the magistrate and eat his seal

effects.log: You find the magistrate and eat the brass of his seal, in front of his clerks. It is not fair to him and it is very funny. The poem gets a second verse.

choices.text: Find the satirist and lie outside the door

effects.log: You find the satirist's house and lie down outside it. The satirist comes out, looks at you, and goes white, and then, being a satirist, laughs. "Well," the satirist says, "you were not in the poem, you know. Only your name." You find you do not mind.

choices.text: Let the poem be

effects.log: You let the poem be. A name is just a name. Still, you are careful, after that, to be a little less like it.

events.text: Long years on, the children in a village you have never visited play a game called Iron-Eater: one child is the beast and walks round eating the others' sticks, and the others must run home before they lose their last one. Nobody can tell you who made it up.

choices.text: Watch from the ridge

effects.log: You watch the game from the ridge all afternoon. The child who is the beast is very good at it: slow, patient, terrifying. You feel strangely proud.

choices.text: Lie down at the edge of the game and be a tree

effects.log: You lie down at the edge of the field and keep very still, and the children decide you are a hill and use you as home. You are safe ground. All afternoon they run to you to be safe from you.

events.text: The new kingdom moves its capital south to Hanyang, below a granite mountain by a wide river. Tens of thousands of workers come down from the provinces to build the walls: stone up the ridges, gates at the four directions. You watch from the ridge above.

choices.text: Watch the walls go up

effects.log: You watch the walls go up all spring, stone by stone along the ridges. They are good walls. You find yourself wondering whether they are meant to keep you out.

choices.text: Carry stone for the masons at night

effects.log: You carry stone for the masons at night, great blocks in your trunk, up the ridges where the carts cannot go. In the morning they find the blocks stacked where they need them, and argue about spirits.

events.text: An official comes up to the ridge with a paper. The new gates need iron: bands, studs, hinges, bolts for four great gates and four small. The new court would be grateful if you could spare some. Or, the paper adds, if you could not, they would be grateful if you stayed out of the city.

choices.text: Give iron for the gates

effects.log: You walk down to the gate-yards and give the iron for all eight gates, out of yourself, a little rusty. The smiths work it all summer. Every gate in the new capital is held together with something you once ate. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Stay out of the city

effects.log: You stay out. The city is built without you, with iron from the mines in the north. You walk round its walls sometimes and do not go in. It is good to be asked. It is also good to say no.

choices.text: Eat the paper's brass seal

effects.log: You eat the seal off the paper and give it back. The official looks at it a long time and then goes down the ridge to explain, very carefully, to somebody important, that the answer was unclear.

events.text: The city is finished. At dusk the great bell at the crossroads rings, and the eight gates close together, and the city is shut for the night. You lie outside the east gate and listen to it ring.

choices.text: Count the strokes

effects.log: Twenty-eight strokes, one for each mansion of the stars, and then the gates close. In the morning you will count thirty-three, one for each heaven, and they will open. You lie there all night between the two numbers.

choices.text: Walk round the walls once, all night

effects.log: You walk all round the outside of the new walls, along the ridges, in one night, the whole circuit. By dawn you know the city by its shape. When the gates open, a guard on the east gate waves to you.

events.text: The new kingdom has a new law: the capital is for scholars and officials, not monks. The temples inside the walls are closing. A line of grey robes walks out of the south gate with bundles, and the guards at the gate count them.

choices.text: Walk beside the monks to the mountains

effects.log: You walk beside the line of monks to the mountains, slowly, at their pace. The guards stop counting. Nobody counts anyone who is walking beside you.

choices.text: Lie down across the south gate

effects.log: You lie down across the south gate. Nobody can go out, and nobody can come in, for a whole day. Then the monks themselves ask you, politely, to move. They have somewhere to be. You move.

events.text: At the crossroads of the new capital they are building a pavilion for a great bell, to be rung when the gates open and close. The bell-founders have dug their pit outside the walls. They are short of metal. Their master looks at you across the pit.

choices.text: Give them the metal for the bell

effects.log: You lie down by the pit and give them what they need: bronze from the temple lamps of the old kingdom, the palace bowls, the incense burners, ten thousand brass spoons. The founders work all night. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Watch, and keep your metal

effects.log: You lie by the pit and watch them melt what they have. It is not quite enough. They make the bell a little thinner than they meant to. It will ring a little higher than they meant to, for a hundred years.

events.text: The pour. The molten bronze runs down the channel into the mould with a sound like a river in spring, and the whole pit glows. The founders' master stands at the edge in a leather coat and does not breathe until it is full.

choices.text: Breathe for the founder

effects.log: You breathe for the founder, slow and deep, until the mould is full. Then the founder breathes out, and so do you, and the whole pit laughs.

choices.text: Look down into the glow

effects.log: You look down into the glow. It is the most beautiful thing you have ever seen: iron that is not eaten but made into something. Something in you that has always been hungry is, for a moment, not.

events.text: The bell is hung in its pavilion at the crossroads and struck for the first time: thirty-three strokes at dawn, and the eight gates of the city open together. The founders' master stands beside you in the crowd with a burned hand wrapped in cloth and tears on their face.

choices.text: Stand very still and listen

effects.log: You stand still. Every stroke goes through you, through every needle and plough and sword you ate, and they all ring with it, very faintly, a little flat. Nobody else hears that. The founder, beside you, does.

choices.text: Ring with it, out loud

effects.log: On the thirty-third stroke you lift your trunk and ring with it, a low iron note under the bronze, and the whole crowd turns. The founder laughs and cries. That note is part of the bell now, people say, ever after.

events.text: Years later the founders' master is old and comes to you at the edge of the city one evening, as the bell rings the gates shut. "It cracked last winter," the founder says. "Only a hair. We have to recast. And I thought, looking at you: there is enough in you for a bell that would never crack."

choices.text: Give enough for the recasting, and stay yourself

effects.log: You give the old founder enough metal for the recasting, and a little more for luck. The new bell rings true. The founder dies that winter, happy, and you lie outside the city on the night of the burial, listening to the bell ring the gates shut.

choices.text: Say no, kindly

effects.log: "Not yet," you say. The old founder nods. "Not yet," the founder agrees. "But you thought about it." You did. You will, again.

choices.text: Lie down in the founders' pit

effects.log: You go out to the founders' pit that night and lie down in it, and tell them to light the fire. You melt slowly, all night, and they pour you into the mould at dawn. For five hundred years you ring the gates of the capital open at dawn and shut at dusk, thirty-three and twenty-eight, very slightly flat.

events.text: The new kingdom counts its monks now: registers, papers, a number for every robe. Temples lose their land. The small ones close. The monks' orders are scattered over the mountains, and every year there are fewer of them on the roads.

choices.text: Visit the closed temples

effects.log: You go round the closed temples, one after another, and lie in their empty courtyards. In some of them an old monk is still living quietly in a back room, and comes out, and is very glad to see you.

choices.text: Eat the iron off the registry office door

effects.log: You eat the iron off the registry office in the provincial town, door and lock and the iron-bound chests. The registers are paper. They survive. The clerk copies them all out again, very slowly, and makes some mistakes on purpose.

events.text: An abbot of your maker's line, too old to walk, must cross the high pass to a temple in the next province before the snow, with the order's scriptures. The novices are carrying the books. Nobody can carry the abbot.

choices.text: Kneel and let the abbot climb on

effects.log: You kneel, and the novices help the old abbot up onto your back, between the hilts, and you carry the abbot over the pass in the first snow, very slowly, as if carrying a full bowl. On the far side the abbot slides down and pats your trunk and does not say thank you, because between you it does not need saying.

choices.text: Clear the pass for them, and let them walk

effects.log: You go ahead and clear the pass, eating the fallen rock and treading the snow flat. The novices carry the abbot in a chair. It takes them a week. They make it.

events.text: At the temple in the next province the abbot, rested, sits with you in the cold courtyard and asks about your maker. "I knew them," the abbot says. "Before. They always dropped their rice. Did they ever tell you the word?"

choices.text: Say that you heard it, and lost it

effects.log: "I heard it," you say. "I cannot find it now." The abbot nods. "It will be at the bottom," the abbot says. "Under everything. It always is." You think about the bottom of you for a long time after.

choices.text: Say nothing, and ask about the maker instead

effects.log: You ask the abbot to tell you about your maker as a novice. The abbot does: clumsy, kind, always late, always dropping rice. You laugh until the needles on your back rattle.

events.text: A new decree: the bells of closed temples are to be collected and melted for coin. Carts come up the mountain roads for them, one temple after another, and the monks stand in the courtyards and watch the bells go.

choices.text: Stand in the road and stop the carts

effects.log: You stand in the road and stop the carts. The carters are not soldiers; they sit down and wait. After a month the officials give up and send the bells back up the mountain. Some of them are hung again. (Hunted +4)

choices.text: Eat the cart axles and let the bells lie

effects.log: You eat the iron axles off every cart on the mountain road, and the bells sit in the road where they stopped. The monks come down at night with ropes and haul them home.

choices.text: Let them go. A bell is only metal

effects.log: You let them go. A bell is only metal, you tell yourself, and you of all things should know. You do not believe it. (Rice -1)

events.text: A provincial lord in the south has made his province into a fist. He taxes the rice to the last grain, hangs anyone who complains in the market, and keeps an armoury of a thousand spears to make sure. The villages send you a message, the only way they can: a bowl of rice, left at every crossroads in the province.

choices.text: Go and look at the armoury

effects.log: You go and look at it. It is a fine armoury, stone-walled, iron-doored, with a thousand spears in racks and the lord's own sword on a stand. The lord is asleep in the house beside it. You can hear him snore.

choices.text: Eat the rice at the crossroads, all of it

effects.log: You eat the rice at every crossroads in the province, bowl by bowl, one night. In the morning the villages find the bowls empty and clean. They understand. So, when he hears about it, does the lord.

events.text: The lord has heard. He doubles the guard on the armoury, and hangs a paper on the door that says the beast is welcome to try. His soldiers stand round it all night with torches, very nervous.

choices.text: Eat the armoury in one night

effects.log: You come in the middle of the night, through the back wall, which is faster than the door. A thousand spears, the iron doors, the racks, the lord's own sword on its stand. The soldiers outside hear chewing for an hour and do not go in. At dawn the lord comes out in his nightclothes with a candle and finds nothing at all.

choices.text: Eat only the lord's own sword

effects.log: You put your trunk through the window and take only the lord's sword off its stand, and eat it while he watches from his bed. It is a small thing. It is the only thing anyone in the province talks about for a year.

choices.text: Leave it to the people of the province

effects.log: You do not go in. This is theirs to do, not yours; a lord brought down by a beast is replaced by another, and a lord brought down by his own people has to be dealt with. You go back to the hills. You hope you are right.

events.text: With no spears the lord's soldiers go home. The villages stop paying. The lord sits alone in his empty house for a month, and then rides north to the capital to complain, and the capital, which has heard about him, does not send him back.

choices.text: Watch who rises after

effects.log: You watch. A council of village headmen, quarrelling, slow, honest. A new magistrate from the capital who is frightened of you and so behaves. It is not good. It is better.

choices.text: Give some of the spears back as ploughs

effects.log: You walk to the biggest smithy in the province and give back the thousand spears, and the smith makes them into ploughs, and that spring the province is ploughed with its tyrant's armoury. People find this very satisfying.

events.text: A cousin of the old lord has found a smith. A new armoury is going up in the next valley, slowly, spear by spear. The villages watch it rise, and look toward the hills where you sleep.

choices.text: Eat the new armoury too

effects.log: You eat it before it is finished. And the next one, two years later. After the third, the cousin gives up and becomes a merchant. You are a little tired of armouries. (Rice -1)

choices.text: Go and lie in front of the smith's door

effects.log: You lie in front of the smith's door. The smith comes out, looks at you, and says, "I have a family." "I know," you say. "Make ploughs." The smith makes ploughs. The cousin cannot find another smith in the whole province.

choices.text: Leave it

effects.log: You leave it. You cannot eat every armoury in the world. The villages will have to learn to do this themselves, and they will, and it will cost them more than it would have cost you.

events.text: Years later, in the province, a children's song about a lord in red nightclothes holding a candle in an empty armoury. It has seven verses, and in the last one the lord is turned into a teapot. None of it is true.

choices.text: Learn the song

effects.log: You learn the song, all seven verses, from a child on a dyke, and hum it on long walks for a century. The teapot verse is the best.

choices.text: Correct the child: he was not a teapot

effects.log: "He was not a teapot," you tell the child. The child looks at you with great scorn. "It is a song," the child says. You are put in your place by a seven-year-old, and it is wonderful.

events.text: Two sects of the murim have gone to war over a mountain with a spring on it. Twenty years of it: ambushes, duels, a disciple killed on a bridge, a revenge for the disciple. Now both sides are gathering on the two banks of the river below the mountain for the battle that will finish it.

choices.text: Lie down in the river between them

effects.log: You lie down in the river between the two banks. The water piles up against you. Both sides look at you across the water. Nobody knows what to do with a beast in the middle of their battle.

choices.text: Go up to the spring and look at it

effects.log: You go up the mountain and look at the spring. It is a very ordinary spring. You drink from it. It is nice water. People have been dying for twenty years over nice water.

events.text: Dawn. Both sects draw. Four hundred swords flash on the two banks, and the masters at the front shout the old insults, and the disciples behind them grip their hilts and do not want to die. You are lying between them.

choices.text: Eat both sides' blades

effects.log: You get up out of the river and go along the first bank, eating, and then the second. Four hundred swords. The masters' famous blades among them. When you lie back down in the river both sects are standing on their banks with nothing in their hands, staring at you. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Ask both masters for their swords

ok.log: You ask, in two dead masters' voices, one from each sect, that they give you their swords and go home. The two masters look at each other across the river for a long time. Then one of them throws a sword into the water in front of you, and the other does too. You eat them both. The disciples sit down on the banks. (Two swords given)

fail.log: You ask. The masters laugh at you. Then they fight, over you, round you, on top of you, for half a day. Nobody dies, because you keep getting in the way. It is still a battle. (-8 health)

choices.text: Stay lying in the river

effects.log: You stay where you are. They fight across you, over the water, and the battle is stupid and short and three disciples are hurt. You lie there and let it happen. It was theirs to do. You are not sure you believe that any more.

events.text: With no swords, the two sects look at each other across the river. Then the younger disciples start throwing stones. Then the older ones start throwing fists. It is a very different kind of war, and much more embarrassing.

choices.text: Let them fight with fists

effects.log: You let them. It is a brawl, muddy and loud, with broken noses and no deaths. At the end of it they are all too tired to hate anyone and sit down on the banks, bleeding a little, and somebody passes round a jar. That is how it ends.

choices.text: Lie down on the bridge so nobody can cross

effects.log: You lie down across the only bridge. They cannot reach each other. They shout across the water until they are hoarse, and then they go home to their own mountains, and the spring is left alone, and in five years nobody can remember why it mattered.

events.text: The two sects have made peace, of a kind: the spring is to belong to both of them, and to neither. A meeting is held on the bridge, and both masters come, empty-handed, and ask you to be the witness.

choices.text: Witness the peace

effects.log: You witness it. You lie across the bridge with one master at your head and one at your tail and they sign the paper on your back. It is the oddest table you will ever be. The peace lasts for years, which in the murim is for ever.

choices.text: Give their swords back as a seal on it

effects.log: You give both masters' swords back, at the end, one to each, in front of everyone, toothmarks on the guards. They look at their swords, and at each other. Neither of them draws. That is the seal.

events.text: The spring on the mountain has a little shrine on it now, put up by both sects together, and in the shrine there is a clumsy carving of you lying in a river with two swords in your mouth.

choices.text: Go and drink from the spring

effects.log: You go up and drink from the spring, and look at the carving. It is terrible. The trunk is too short and the eyes are huge. You like it very much.

choices.text: Leave the shrine alone

effects.log: You leave it alone. A shrine is for the people who make it, not the thing in it. But you walk past the mountain sometimes, at a distance, to see that it is still there.

events.text: The Demonic Cult sends an envoy to the hills where you sleep: a polite person in black with a box. In the box, on red silk, a blade the colour of a coal, humming faintly. "Our master's gift," the envoy says. "The Blood Blade. It cuts everything. It would be happiest in you."

choices.text: Look at it a long time

effects.log: You look at it a long time. It is the most beautiful weapon you have ever seen and the rice in your tail has gone cold at the sight of it. The envoy waits, smiling.

choices.text: Send the envoy away at once

effects.log: You turn your back. The envoy closes the box, bows, and goes. "Our master will ask again," the envoy says over a shoulder. "Our master always asks again."

events.text: The cult's master comes in person, at night, to a mountain top, and holds the Blood Blade out over a bonfire so that you can see yourself in it, red. "Power," the master says. "More than all the others together. It will only cost you a little of what is in your tail."

choices.text: Take the Blood Blade

effects.log: You take it. It goes down hot and stays hot, and something in your tail shrinks from it, the way a hand shrinks from a stove. You are stronger than you have ever been. You feel smaller. (Relic: the Blood Blade, Rice -3)

choices.text: Say no

effects.log: "No," you say. The master shrugs and sheathes the blade. "Next century," the master says, and goes. The rice in your tail warms again slowly, like hands after snow. (Rice +1)

choices.text: Eat the bonfire's iron trivet and leave

effects.log: You eat the iron trivet out of the bonfire, which collapses in sparks, and walk away down the mountain without a word. Behind you the cult master laughs, delighted, for a long time. You have the feeling you have made a fan.

events.text: The Blood Blade talks in you at night. Not like the other voices: it does not remember an owner. It only wants. It wants you to go and eat the next sect, and the next, and stop asking.

choices.text: Listen to it, a little

effects.log: You listen to it, a little. It is easy to listen to. You eat a whole sect's armoury that winter without asking, and feel nothing at all until spring. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Bury it under the other voices

effects.log: You put it at the bottom, under all the old owners of the swords, and ask them to sit on it. They do. It is quieter. It is never quiet.

choices.text: Cough it up into the river

effects.log: You cough the Blood Blade up into a deep river and let it go down into the dark. The cult will find it. They always do. But it is not in you. (Rice +2)

events.text: The cult's envoy comes back, the same polite person in black, greyer now. "Our master asks again," the envoy says, "as promised." The box is in their hands. Behind them, on the road, a whole province of the cult's soldiers waits to see what you will do.

choices.text: Eat the soldiers' weapons on the road

effects.log: You walk past the envoy and down the road and eat the cult soldiers' weapons, all of them, while the envoy watches with the box in their hands. At the end you come back. "No," you say. The envoy bows, with real respect, and goes. (Hunted +3)

choices.text: Take the Blood Blade, this time

effects.log: You take it. The envoy seems almost sad. It goes down hot. (Relic: the Blood Blade, Rice -3)

choices.text: Say no again, politely

effects.log: "No," you say, "thank you." The envoy laughs, a real laugh. "Every century," the envoy says. "Until one of us is tired." You are not tired. (Rice +1)

events.text: A ship from across the eastern sea brings the king a gift: an elephant, a real one, the first the kingdom has ever seen. The whole capital goes to look. They say it is grey and wrinkled and sad, and eats four times what a horse eats. They say it is about your size, when you were younger.

choices.text: Go and look at it from the wall

effects.log: You look at it over the stable wall. It looks back at you. It is the first creature you have ever met that is not afraid of you, and it is not afraid of anything else either, only very far from home.

choices.text: Stay away. Two of you would be too many

effects.log: You stay away. Two enormous grey things with trunks in one capital is too many for the capital, you think. You hear it calling at night sometimes, on the wind.

events.text: An official went to the elephant's stable and mocked it, and spat on it, and it killed him. The court is debating the elephant's crime. A minister has proposed that, as one would not execute it, it should be exiled, like a disgraced official, to an island in the south.

choices.text: Listen to the debate from outside the hall

effects.log: You listen at the back wall of the hall. The ministers debate whether an elephant can be guilty, and whether a beast can be exiled, and you find yourself listening very carefully. Nobody looks at the wall.

choices.text: Go and lie outside the elephant's stable

effects.log: You lie down outside the stable at night. The elephant lies down on the other side of the wall. Neither of you sleeps much.

events.text: The elephant is on its island in the south now, with orders from the king that it be kept fed and given good water and grass, so that it does not sicken. Nobody else visits it. It stands on the shore at evening and looks at the sea.

choices.text: Swim out to visit it

effects.log: You swim out through the surf, which is hard work for iron, and come up the shore beside it. It puts its trunk on your trunk. It smells of grass and salt and very great loneliness. You stay a season. When you swim back, it stands on the shore and watches you all the way to the mainland.

choices.text: Stand on the mainland shore where it can see you

effects.log: You stand on the mainland shore every evening for a season, where it can see you across the strait. It sees you. It stands on its shore. It is not much. It is not nothing.

events.text: You lay down for a long rest after the new capital, and woke up a hill. Rust has crusted over the needles on your back, and soil has blown onto the rust, and grass has grown in the soil, and now there are young pines rooted in you. You can feel their roots, like a tickle.

choices.text: Lie still and let them grow

effects.log: You lie still. The pines grow. A woodpecker moves in. Some years you forget you are anything but a hill, and those are the best years.

choices.text: Shake them off and stand up

effects.log: You stand up, and the pines slide off you in a roar of soil, and the valley below thinks it is an earthquake. You feel very light, and a little lonely without them.

events.text: Hunters walk up a path that goes over your back, three of them, talking about deer. They do not know they are walking on the Iron-Eater. One of them sits down on your eye to eat lunch.

choices.text: Keep very still until they go

effects.log: You keep very still. They eat lunch on your eyelid and talk about deer and their wives and their debts, and go on over the top of you. You learn more about the province in an afternoon than in a century.

choices.text: Blink

effects.log: You blink. The hunter on your eyelid goes up in the air and comes down running. All three of them run, all the way home, and tell everybody, and nobody believes them. The path over you is not used for a long time.

events.text: You are as big as you will ever be. You can feel it: the iron goes in and does not make you more any more. You are a hill, and hills do not grow. For the first time since a needle on a sewing cushion, eating is only eating.

choices.text: Eat less, then

effects.log: You eat less. Then less again. A decade without eating anything but what the rain washes into your mouth. You do not shrink. You are a little surprised at how good it feels.

choices.text: Keep eating out of habit

effects.log: You keep eating, out of habit, a little here and there. It changes nothing in you and something in every village you eat from. You know that. You do it anyway, sometimes. (Rice -1)

choices.text: Wonder what you are for, if not to grow

effects.log: You lie on the hillside and wonder what you are for, if not to grow. It is a long question. The pines on your back have no opinion.

events.text: A wet decade. The monsoon comes early and stays late, ten years running, and you lie on your hillside in it, and rust. Orange water runs down your flanks into the paddies below. You are a little less of you every year.

choices.text: Go into the old mine and stay dry

effects.log: You go deep into the old mine and stay there, dry, ten years. You do not rust. You also do not see the sky for years, and when you come out you blink like a mole.

choices.text: Lie in the rain and let it take what it takes

effects.log: You lie in the rain. It takes what it takes: a little iron, a little of the edge of you, the sharpness of some of the needles. What is left is smoother. The farmers below say the orange water is good for the rice, which is not true, and the rice grows well anyway.

events.text: The rust running off you has stained a whole valley orange: the stones in the stream, the walls of the paddies, the feet of the farmers. They call it the Iron-Eater's valley and the children have orange toes all summer.

choices.text: Move to a drier hill

effects.log: You move to a drier hill, slowly, over a season. The valley stays orange for years. The children are a little disappointed.

choices.text: Stay. They seem to like it

effects.log: You stay. The farmers start dyeing cloth in the stream, a fine rust-orange, and it sells. You have become, without meaning to, an industry.

events.text: Water is the one thing you cannot eat. You have known it since your first rains on the hillside. Now you lie in the rain and think about what water does to iron: not all at once, not by force, a little at a time, for ever.

choices.text: Think about it the way water would

effects.log: You think about it the way water would: not all at once. You have spent your whole life all at once. You try, for a decade, to do one small thing a year. It is very difficult. It is very restful.

choices.text: Decide that you will not be worn away

effects.log: You decide that you will not be worn away. You eat a mountain of ore in a year to stay the size you are. It works. It is exhausting. You do not know whom you are proving it to.

events.text: The farmers of the orange valley come up the hill in a body after the wet decade and lay something at your feet: a straw raincoat, enormous, woven by the whole valley over a winter, big enough to cover a hill.

choices.text: Wear it

effects.log: You let them put it over you. It takes forty people and a day. Under it you are dry for the first time in years. You keep it on until it rots, and then the valley weaves another.

choices.text: Thank them, and give it to their granary roof

effects.log: You push it gently back down the hill to the valley's granary, which leaks, and they put it on the granary roof instead. The rice stays dry for years. That is the better use, and you all know it.

events.text: You come back to the pine ridge where the Azure Dragon sleeps, the first time in a very long time. The old mine is still there. So are the stakes: new ones, driven into the crest in the night by men with mallets who want to cut the ridge's vein, so that no great person will ever be born under it.

choices.text: Eat the new stakes

effects.log: You eat them, every one, before dawn, like barley sugar. The ridge breathes out. Something in the cloud above it opens one green-gold eye, looks at you, and closes it again, satisfied.

choices.text: Go into the old mine and say hello

effects.log: You go into the old mine, and lie down in your old place, and say hello to the ridge. The ridge says hello back in the form of a light warm rain on the pines. It remembers you.

events.text: The vein-cutters come back at night with more stakes. They are paid by someone in the capital who is afraid of what might be born under this ridge. They drive the stakes in by lantern-light, very fast, looking over their shoulders.

choices.text: Wait until they finish, then eat them all

effects.log: You wait until they finish, then come out of the mine and eat the whole night's work in front of them. They watch, then drop their mallets and run. You eat the mallets' iron rings too.

choices.text: Lie across the crest so there is nowhere to drive them

effects.log: You lie along the whole crest of the ridge. There is nowhere to drive a stake that is not you. The vein-cutters stand at the foot of the ridge with their bundles and argue, and go home.

events.text: The ridge speaks, in weather, the way it always has. A warm rain, a mist in the morning, a single roll of thunder far off. You understand more of it now than you did. It is saying: you are welcome here, for as long as you like. Small or large.

choices.text: Ask what it means by small

effects.log: You ask, and the ridge answers in a thin mist that settles on you and runs off, and takes a very little of you with it, and gives it back as ore in the seam. You understand: if you wanted to be small again, here, you could be.

choices.text: Thank it and go back to the world

effects.log: You thank it, in the only way you know, by pulling one more stake that nobody has found, and go back to the world. The ridge sends a rain after you, for a mile, like someone waving.

events.text: Morning on the ridge. A stake in your mouth, the vein-cutters running down the hill, the seam cold and wet in the old mine behind you, and a light rain falling on exactly you. You could stay. You could give back most of what you are to the world, and be small again here, gnawing the mountain, for ever.

choices.text: Stay a while, and then go on

effects.log: You stay a decade, small in your heart if not in your body, eating stakes and ore. Then you go on. The ridge does not mind. It knows you will come back.

choices.text: Go back to the world now

effects.log: You go back down to the world. It needs you, or thinks it does, and you are not ready to be small. The rain follows you to the foot of the ridge and stops.

choices.text: Give back the world's iron and stay small, for ever

effects.log: You open your mouth at the foot of the ridge and give it all back, to the valley, to the smiths, to the market towns, until you are only as big as a dog again. Then you go up into the old mine and gnaw the mountain, and eat the vein-cutters' stakes by morning. You are the happiest creature in the province, and the ridge sleeps very well on top of you.

events.text: A dry winter. From your hill you can see the capital's main palace below the granite mountain, and one night you see a glow in it where there should not be one. Then a line of glow along a roof. Then the whole of one hall standing up in fire against the dark.

choices.text: Go down to the palace

effects.log: You go down the mountain at a run, the fastest you have moved in a century. Behind you the pines shake on your back. The city gate is open; everyone is running out of it; nobody stops you running in.

choices.text: Watch from the hill

effects.log: You watch from the hill. It is not your palace. It is not your fire. You tell yourself this until the second hall catches, and then you are already running.

events.text: The palace courtyard. Courtiers running with lanterns and ledgers, court ladies with their skirts held up, guards passing buckets from a well that is already dry. Three halls burning. The heat comes off them like a wall. Your tail is still rice.

choices.text: Walk into the fire and eat it

effects.log: You walk into the burning hall and open your mouth, and the fire goes into you. It is like drinking a river of hot broth. It does not burn you. It feeds you. You eat the whole hall's fire, beam by beam, and walk out of the ash into the courtyard, and the courtiers fall on their faces. Fire is food. (Heat +25)

choices.text: Draw the fire in through your trunk from outside

effects.log: You stand outside the burning hall, tail tucked tight, and draw the fire in through your trunk like a river into a cave. It goes in. It keeps going in. It does not hurt. By dawn the hall is standing, black and smoking, and whole. Fire is food. (Heat +20)

choices.text: Pull the people out first

effects.log: You go along the burning halls pulling people out with your trunk: a clerk, a cook, an old lady-in-waiting who will not leave her birds. The halls burn down. Everyone in them lives. You still have not eaten a fire. You have done something else.

events.text: Morning. The palace smokes. The king stands in the courtyard in borrowed robes, looking at the black halls, and then at you, lying in the ash with smoke coming out of your trunk. The whole court is waiting to see what he will say.

choices.text: Lower your head to the king

effects.log: You lower your head. The king looks at you a long time. "We were told to burn you," he says. "My grandfather's court had a book about it." He laughs, without much humour. "We will rebuild. Come back when we do." You will.

choices.text: Get up and go before he speaks

effects.log: You get up and go, through the ash, out of the gate, before anyone can say anything. Some things are better left without a speech. The court writes it down anyway, in the annals, in very careful words.

events.text: They rebuild the halls the next year, quickly. The master carpenter has heard about you, and puts a little carved beast with a trunk on the end of one roof ridge, among the other guardians, where it can watch for sparks.

choices.text: Go and look at the carving

effects.log: You go and look at it from the gate. It is very small and very fierce. You feel something you have never felt before, which turns out to be pride.

choices.text: Sleep on the palace hill every dry winter after

effects.log: You sleep on the hill above the palace every dry winter after that, just in case. Nobody asks you to. The palace does not burn again for years.

events.text: Something has changed in you since the palace. You used to be iron with a little rice at the end. Now there is something else in you too, a warmth in the middle of the iron that does not go out, like the last coal in a stove in the morning.

choices.text: Sit with it

effects.log: You sit with it. It is the fire you ate. It is not angry any more. It is just warm, and it is yours.

choices.text: Go and find another fire to eat

effects.log: You go and find another fire: a forest burning on a hillside in the autumn. You walk into it and eat it to the last spark. You are getting the taste for it.

events.text: A great army has crossed the sea from the islands in the east and landed in the south, with guns that the kingdom has never seen in such numbers. They are marching north up the roads, very fast, and every city they reach falls. The king has left the capital in the rain.

choices.text: Go south down the road toward them

effects.log: You go south down the main road, against the stream of everyone else. Carts, families, soldiers without officers. Nobody looks at you twice. There are worse things on the roads this year.

choices.text: Go north after the king

effects.log: You go north after the king, through the rain, up the long road. He has very few people with him. You walk behind them a week, and nobody follows them, because nobody follows something that has you behind it.

events.text: The capital is burning. All its palaces, and the archives, and the great streets. Some of it the invaders lit; some of it the city's own people lit, angry at a court that ran. The smoke goes up for days.

choices.text: Walk into the burning city and eat the fire

effects.log: You walk into the burning city and eat fire for three days. Halls, archives, streets. You cannot eat all of it; it is a whole city. But you eat the fire off the archive halls first, and the annals of the old kings come out of the ash scorched and whole. (Heat +30)

choices.text: Stand at the gate and get people out

effects.log: You stand at the south gate and carry people out of the smoke in your trunk and on your back, all day, all night, until there is nobody left to carry. The city burns. The people mostly do not.

events.text: On the roads south of the capital the invaders' columns march with their guns on their shoulders: long iron barrels, thousands of them, the best iron you have ever smelled. The roads are long and narrow and run through the mountains.

choices.text: Eat the guns on the roads, column by column

effects.log: You come down on the road at night, from the mountain, and eat the guns: barrels, locks, ramrods, the iron of the carts. Column after column, for a season. The invaders stop marching at night. Then they stop marching on that road at all.

choices.text: Eat only their powder-carts' iron

effects.log: You eat only the iron bands off the powder carts, so that the barrels split and the powder spills in the mud and the rain. It is slow and careful and very effective. The guns are silent for a month.

choices.text: Lie across the road

effects.log: You lie across the mountain road, all of you, a hill where no hill was. The columns stop, and go back, and find another road, which is a week longer. A week, in that war, is a great deal.

events.text: The monks have risen. From every mountain temple the grey robes come down with staves and banners, old men and novices, thousands of them, answering the call of an old master in the north. Nobody expected it. The court that closed their temples did not expect it most of all.

choices.text: March with the monk army

effects.log: You march with them. Nobody asks you to; you simply fall in at the back of the column, and the novices at the back look round at you and then grin. You are the slowest thing in the army, and the safest.

choices.text: Go ahead of them and eat what is waiting

effects.log: You go ahead of the monks along the roads, and eat what is waiting for them: ambushes, gun positions, the iron of fortress gates. When the monks arrive, the way is open.

events.text: The war goes on for years. It comes back after a truce, worse. You learn to live in it: to eat what you can, guns and gates and the iron of the invaders' ships at the river mouths, and to carry what you can, people and books and the bones of the old palaces.

choices.text: Keep eating the war

effects.log: You keep eating the war, year after year, until you can taste it in your sleep. It is not food. It is just iron. But every barrel you eat is a barrel that is not fired, and you count them.

choices.text: Keep carrying people

effects.log: You keep carrying people. Families over passes, children across rivers, the wounded to the temples. You never count them. Somebody else does: a monk with a ledger, who writes your name at the top of a very long list.

events.text: The war ends at last, as wars do, more because everyone is tired than because anyone has won. The ships go back across the sea. The country is ash and graves and empty fields. And all over it, in the mud of the roads, there are guns, and swords, and spears that nobody wants any more.

choices.text: Eat the war's leftovers, all of them

effects.log: You walk the length of the kingdom eating the war's leftovers, every barrel and blade in every ditch, so that no child will pick one up. It takes years. At the end there is not a gun lying in a field anywhere in the kingdom.

choices.text: Give the iron to the smiths for ploughs

effects.log: You give the iron of the war to the smiths, all of it, and they make ploughs, and the first spring after the war the fields are ploughed with guns. The farmers say the rice tastes of nothing in particular, which is how rice should taste.

events.text: The monk general comes up the hill alone: a stern monk in a kasaya over armour, a disciple of the old master who called the temples to war. In his hand is a plain staff with an iron tip, and you know it the moment you smell it. A staff of your maker's line.

choices.text: Stand still and let him come

effects.log: You stand still. He comes right up to you and stops, the staff grounded beside him. "I could stop you," he says. "One blow. You know that." You know that. "I am not here to stop you."

choices.text: Back away from the staff

effects.log: You back away, the whole hill of you, from a man with a stick. He sees it, and something in his face softens. "No," he says. "Not today. Come back."

events.text: "I am asking you to march," the monk general says. "Not to fight. You do not need to fight. Walk in front of us, and the guns will break on you, and my monks will live who otherwise would die. That is all."

choices.text: March in front of the monk army

effects.log: You march in front of them for a season. The guns break on you, the arrows break on you, the iron you eat, and behind you the monks come through alive who otherwise would not. At night the novices sleep against your flanks for warmth.

choices.text: Refuse. You will not be anyone's wall

effects.log: You refuse. The monk general nods. "A wall that chooses," he says. "Good. Better than a wall that is told." He goes back down the hill to his monks, who march without you, and some of them die, and you think about that for a long time.

events.text: After a battle, the monk general sits with you on the hill and shows you the staff. "Your maker's line," he says. "There are three of these left in the kingdom. One blow, and you give back everything and go. I will tell you where the other two are. In case one day you want them."

choices.text: Listen, and remember

effects.log: He tells you: a temple in the far south, a hermitage on the eastern coast. You remember both. You hope you will never need them. You are no longer sure you hope that.

choices.text: Tell him your tail is a second way

effects.log: You lay your tail on the grass in front of him and tell him the other way: fire, at the rice. He looks at it a long time. "Two ways," he says. "And both of them gifts, if you choose them." He will not tell anyone. You know he will not.

events.text: The war is over. The monk general is old and is going across the sea as an envoy, to bring back the kingdom's captives. Before he goes he comes up your hill one last time with the staff, and stands there a while, and then lays it down on the grass.

choices.text: Leave the staff where he laid it

effects.log: You leave it. He picks it up again, after a long time, and nods, and goes. "Kept," he says. "For when it is wanted." You both know what that means.

choices.text: Ask him to take it with him across the sea

effects.log: You ask him to take it with him, far away, across the sea. He laughs. "So you cannot find it? Or so you can?" He takes it. He brings it back, years later. It is in the temple where he dies.

events.text: In the second year of the war's return, the pavilion at the capital's crossroads burns, and the great bell falls out of it into the ash and cracks. No more twenty-eight strokes at dusk. No more thirty-three at dawn. The city opens and shuts without a sound.

choices.text: Go and look at the cracked bell

effects.log: You go and look at it in the ash. It is cracked from lip to shoulder. You remember the founders' pit, if you were there, or you remember hearing it from the hills, which is almost the same. It has rung over you for generations.

choices.text: Lift it out of the ash

effects.log: You lift it out of the ash with your trunk and set it upright on the stones, so that at least it is not lying down. Nobody asked you to. The people of the crossroads come out and stand round it and touch it.

events.text: The cracked bell is useless. Nobody has the bronze to recast it; the war has eaten everything. You could eat it. You could hold its metal for the kingdom until there is a kingdom again to give it back to.

choices.text: Eat it, to keep it

effects.log: You eat the bell, slowly, in the ash, while the people of the crossroads watch. It goes down like an old song. You will keep it. You tell them so, in a founder's voice. They believe you.

choices.text: Leave it standing in the ash

effects.log: You leave it standing in the ash. A cracked bell is still a bell. People come and tap it sometimes for luck, and it makes a dull short sound, and they smile.

events.text: Peace, and a new pavilion going up at the crossroads, and the founders looking for metal for a new bell. They look at you, because everyone knows what you ate.

choices.text: Give the bell back

effects.log: You give it back, whole, in the founders' yard, the same bronze, crack and all. They melt it and pour it again. When it rings, the old people at the crossroads say it sounds exactly like before, and cry.

choices.text: Keep it. It is safer in you

effects.log: You keep it. The founders cast a smaller bell from other bronze. It rings a little higher. The old people say it is not the same. You know it is not. (Rice -2)

events.text: Since you began to eat fire you are warm all the time, and some years you are hot: red at the needle-tips, steaming in the rain. Everything you touch scorches. You lie down in a meadow and get up from a field of ash.

choices.text: Lie in a stream to cool

effects.log: You lie down in a mountain stream and the water boils round you. A fisherman on the bank stares, and then, being a fisherman, notices that all the fish downstream are cooked, and fetches a basket.

choices.text: Keep to bare rock in the hot years

effects.log: You keep to the bare granite of the mountains in the years you are hot, where there is nothing to burn. It is lonely up there. The rock is warm for a mile round you, and the mountain goats come in winter to stand on it.

events.text: A village in the hills asks you, through a very brave grandmother, if you would sleep near the village in the winter. The winters are cold, and the wood is scarce, and you are warm.

choices.text: Sleep beside the village all winter

effects.log: You sleep at the edge of the village all winter, as close as you dare. The snow melts in a ring round you. The village keeps its doors open toward you and saves half its firewood. The grandmother sits against your flank in the evenings and knits.

choices.text: Say you are afraid you will burn it

effects.log: "I am afraid I will burn it," you say. The grandmother nods. "Then sleep on the far side of the stream," she says. "We will come to you." All winter the village comes over the ice to warm its hands.

events.text: The first fire you eat on purpose, for no reason except that it is there: a grass fire on a hillside in autumn, small, harmless, going nowhere. You eat it anyway, and it is delicious, and nobody needed you to.

choices.text: Admit to yourself that you enjoyed it

effects.log: You admit it. It was not duty. It was delicious. You lie on the burned hillside feeling greedy and warm and oddly happy.

choices.text: Promise yourself to eat only fires that would hurt someone

effects.log: You promise. Only fires that would hurt someone. It is a good rule. It means you spend a great deal of time watching fires that will not hurt anyone, hungrily.

events.text: From the moment you became the Eater of Fire, heat is no longer a danger in you. It is food. It goes into you and turns into strength, like rice turning into a farmer. The hot years are over. You are warm, and you will stay warm.

choices.text: Lie in the sun and digest

effects.log: You lie in the sun on a granite slope for a whole year and digest every fire you have ever eaten. It turns into something quiet and deep in you, like a well.

choices.text: Go and find the village that sent the grandmother

effects.log: You go back to the hill village. It is winter. You lie down right beside it, closer than ever before, and nothing catches. The grandmother's grandchildren climb on you and slide down your flank in the snow.

events.text: There is a village by the river that has given up iron so that you will pass it by. Wooden ploughs with fire-hardened tips. Clay pots. Bone needles. Hinges of rope, locks of oak, a well with a wooden bucket. Not one nail.

choices.text: Walk past on the far side of the river

effects.log: You walk past on the far side of the river, as they meant you to. A farmer pulling a wooden plough stops and watches you go the whole way, and does not wave, and does not look away.

choices.text: Cross the river and walk through the village

effects.log: You cross the river and walk through the village, slowly, touching nothing. There is nothing to touch. People stand in their doorways and watch you sniff at their wooden ploughs and clay pots and go out the other side. They are not sure whether they have won.

events.text: The wooden village is poor. Wooden ploughs break in stony ground; clay pots crack; the harvest is half what the next valley's is. They have done it for fear of you, for generations. The children have never seen a needle.

choices.text: Leave a heap of good iron at their gate

effects.log: You leave a heap of good iron at their gate one night: ploughs, pots, needles. In the morning they look at it and argue all day. In the end they take it in. The next harvest is twice the last.

choices.text: Tell them they do not have to

effects.log: You stand at their gate and tell them, in a farmer's voice, that they do not have to do this, that you will not come. They listen politely. They do not believe you. It takes another generation for them to buy their first iron plough.

events.text: Long years on, the wooden village is famous for it. People come from the capital to see the village with no iron, and buy little wooden ploughs as keepsakes. The village has an iron plough now, hidden in a barn, and everyone pretends not to know.

choices.text: Pretend not to know, too

effects.log: You pretend not to know. You walk past on the far side of the river every spring, for the tourists, and the village is very grateful.

choices.text: Eat the hidden plough, just once, as a joke

effects.log: You eat the hidden plough one night, as a joke, and leave a better one in its place. The village laughs for a year. They put the joke in their song.

events.text: In a mountain temple an old monk reads you a story from a very old sutra, because, the monk says, you ought to know where you come from. A king once bought a strange beast called the Mother of Calamity, that ate needles and grew, and burned the town that tried to kill it with fire.

choices.text: Listen to the whole story

effects.log: You listen. The beast in the story ate needles, then iron, then grew too big, and the town set it on fire, and it ran through the streets burning, and the town burned, and the kingdom with it. The monk rolls up the scroll. "That is the warning," the monk says. "You are the answer to it, if you want to be."

choices.text: Ask whether it is a story about you

effects.log: "Is it about me?" you ask. "It is about what you would be," the monk says, "if nobody had ever made you out of supper." You think about that all night.

events.text: There is a second story in the old monk's scrolls: a beast from far away in the west of the world that licks iron and copper and keeps away evil, whose picture people hang on screens to sleep well. The monk shows you the picture. It looks a little like you, and a little like a bear, and a little like nothing.

choices.text: Wonder if you could keep away evil

effects.log: You wonder about it all winter. Not eating iron; eating what makes people afraid. You do not know how yet. But you are, after all, very good at eating.

choices.text: Laugh at the picture

effects.log: You laugh at the picture. It is a very bad likeness. The monk laughs too. "The painters never met one," the monk says. "Now they could meet you, and do better."

events.text: You have been two things, the old stories say: the Mother of Calamity, that grows until it burns the world, and the beast that keeps calamity away. The same mouth. You lie on your hill and think about which of them has been eating lately.

choices.text: Count your calamities and your kindnesses

effects.log: You count. The ploughs, the villages without tools, the burned thatch. The armies with empty hands, the cells with no locks. It is not even. You are not sure which side is longer. You decide to make it longer on one side.

choices.text: Decide it does not matter which you were

effects.log: You decide it does not matter which you were. It matters what you eat tomorrow. That is easier to think about, and harder to do.

events.text: Long years on, you go back to the old general's grave. It is still red, still bare, in a green hillside. People come to look at it. They bring nothing. That is the custom, they tell each other: you bring nothing to the grave of a man who looked on gold as stone.

choices.text: Bring nothing, and lie down beside it

effects.log: You bring nothing and lie down beside it, a hill beside a grave. The people coming up the path stop, and look, and bow to both of you. You are not sure you deserve it.

choices.text: Ask the sword in you if it wants to see

effects.log: You ask the general's sword in you, and it says nothing, as he would have. But you feel it settle, a little, the way a man settles in a chair at home.

events.text: A greedy official comes to the red grave with a crowd behind him, to show he is not afraid of it, and makes a speech about the old general's foolishness. Gold is gold, he says. Only a fool looks on it as stone.

choices.text: Eat the gold off his belt in front of the crowd

effects.log: You eat the gold off his belt, and the gold rings off his fingers, and the gold pin out of his hat, in front of everyone, very slowly. Then you look at him as if he were stone. The crowd goes home very happy.

choices.text: Let him finish and say nothing

effects.log: You let him finish. You say nothing. Nobody in the crowd says anything either. He walks back down the path into the silence, and you can see him feel it. That is enough.

events.text: The general's sword talks in you one night, for the first time, in his voice: short, dry, a soldier's. "Do not give me back," it says. "There is nobody to give me to. Keep me. And when you are tired, stop."

choices.text: Promise to stop when you are tired

effects.log: You promise. It is the second promise you have made to an old soldier. The voice says, "Good," and nothing else for a long time.

choices.text: Ask him how he knew when to stop

effects.log: "How did you know when to stop?" you ask. "I did not," says the sword. "They stopped me. Do better." You lie awake until morning.

events.text: You go back to the house with the attic, the first time in a very long time. Different people live there: the descendants of the ones who hid your maker. They know the story. It is the family's story. An old woman comes out into the yard and looks up at you, and up, and up.

choices.text: Rest your trunk on the roof ridge

effects.log: You rest your trunk on the roof ridge, very gently, so as not to break the tiles. The old woman laughs. "It was smaller in the story," she says. "It fitted on a palm."

choices.text: Lie down outside the gate, as you used to

effects.log: You lie down outside the gate. The children come out one at a time to look at you, and the bravest one feeds you a nail, because that is what happens in the story.

events.text: The family is poor this year: a flood, a bad harvest, a debt to a moneylender in town. The old woman of the house does not ask you for anything. She would rather die. But the children are thin.

choices.text: Eat the moneylender's strongbox

effects.log: You go into town and eat the moneylender's strongbox in the night, lock, hinges, iron bands and all. The paper debts inside fall out on the floor in a heap and get mixed up beyond sorting. The family's debt is never found again. Nor is anyone else's. (Hunted +3)

choices.text: Give them a plough and a pot and a good knife

effects.log: You give them a plough, a pot and a good knife, out of yourself, the best you have. The old woman looks at them a long time and then says, "Well. You owe us." That is the end of the argument.

events.text: The attic is still there under the thatch. One of the children climbs up and finds, in a crack between the floorboards, three grains of rice, dry as stone, very old. They bring them down in a cupped hand to show you.

choices.text: Ask them to put the grains back

effects.log: You ask them to put the grains back exactly where they found them. They do, very carefully, with tweezers made of bamboo. You do not know why it matters. It matters.

choices.text: Look at them a long time, and say nothing

effects.log: You look at them a long time, three grains on a small palm. Something in your tail answers them. The child closes the hand gently and keeps them for the rest of their life in a little box.

events.text: Still red-hot from a fire, and the road home runs through a market town of thatch on market day.

choices.text: Go round by the river, however long it takes

effects.log: You go round by the river. It takes a week. The river steams the whole way and the fish downstream are very surprised. Not one roof catches.

choices.text: Go straight through, fast

effects.log: You go straight through, fast. The thatch catches behind you, stall after stall. The town will remember market day for years. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Lie down in the reservoir until you cool

effects.log: You lie down in the town's reservoir until you stop boiling it. It takes a month and the town has to carry water from the river. They grumble. Nothing burns.

events.text: A smiths' petition again, a new generation of smiths: their grandfathers' list of ploughs you owe, copied out neatly and nailed to a tree on your road.

choices.text: Give back what is on the list

effects.log: You give back what is on the list, plough by plough, at the smithy door. The young smiths cross it off. One of them adds a line at the bottom: paid.

choices.text: Leave the list on the tree

effects.log: You leave it on the tree. It is an old debt. The smiths are not starving. But you walk past that tree for a long time with your head down. (Rice -1)

events.text: A village has left a heap of broken iron on a straw mat outside its gate, and a bowl of rice beside it, as the villages do now: a toll, a gift, a prayer.

choices.text: Eat the iron and the rice and pass by

effects.log: You eat both and pass by. The village sleeps well that year.

choices.text: Eat the rice and leave the iron

effects.log: You eat the rice and leave the iron. The headman looks at the untouched heap in the morning and understands, and takes it to the smithy to be made into something.

events.text: A hunter with a torch, following you through the woods, a long way back. They still come, every generation, the ones who have read the old book. Waiting for you to sleep.

choices.text: Turn round and look at the hunter

effects.log: You turn round and look at the hunter, the whole hill of you, for a long time. The torch goes out. The hunter goes home and burns the book.

choices.text: Sleep in the river with your tail under water

effects.log: You sleep in the river with your tail under the water, as you have learned to. The hunter waits on the bank all night with a useless torch, and leaves a bowl of rice on the bank in the morning, as an apology, or a joke.

events.text: Disciples of a sect whose sword is in your belly come up your valley in white, in a line, to ask for it back. They do not draw. They kneel at the foot of the valley and wait.

choices.text: Give the sword back

effects.log: You walk down to them and give it back, whole, toothmarks on the guard. They take it away up the mountain singing. You feel lighter by exactly one sword, and by more than that. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Keep it, and let them kneel

effects.log: You keep it. They kneel all day, and go home at dusk, and come back next year, and the year after. (Rice -1)

events.text: A granary is burning in a valley below you, at night. The farmers are passing buckets. The fire is winning.

choices.text: Go down and eat the fire

effects.log: You go down and eat it, beam by beam, until the granary stands black and smoking with the rice inside it scorched on top and good underneath. The farmers sit down in the mud. One of them starts to laugh and cannot stop.

choices.text: Let the farmers handle it

effects.log: You let them handle it. They save half the granary. It is their granary, and half is not nothing, and they did it. You are not sure that was a kindness.

events.text: Children have found out that they can climb you. On fine days there are a dozen of them on your back, sliding down your flank on sacks, getting lost among the pines, being called home at dusk by mothers in the valley.

choices.text: Lie very still all day

effects.log: You lie very still all day. At dusk the last child slides off and runs home. You have been a hill for a whole day, and a good one.

choices.text: Shake, very gently, to make them shriek

effects.log: You shake, very gently, once. Twelve children shriek with delight and cling on. It becomes the thing children do: climb the Iron-Eater and wait for the shake.

events.text: The leader of a sect at war, {npc}, comes alone up your hill with the sect's sword in both hands. "Take it," {he} says. "If it is in you, there is nothing left for us to fight for. Please."

choices.text: Take it, given

effects.log: You take it from {his} hands, gently. {npc} stands there empty-handed for a long time, and then laughs, like someone putting down a heavy load. The war ends that autumn. (A sword given)

choices.text: Tell {him} to bring the other side's sword too

effects.log: "Bring theirs too," you say. {npc} stares, and then goes down the hill, and comes back a month later with the other sect's leader, and two swords. You eat them both. Two leaders sit on your foot and drink together. (Two swords given)

events.text: A grandmaster, {npc}, has climbed your hill to make you an offer: {he} wants to be the one blade you cannot eat. {He} draws a sword so fine it is almost invisible and holds it out. "Try," {he} says.

choices.text: Try to eat it

ok.log: You close your mouth on the blade. It cuts your tongue, a little. Then it goes down. {npc} looks at {his} empty hand for a long time, and then bows to you, deeply. "I had to know," {he} says. (A sword taken)

fail.log: You close your mouth on it, and it is not there. It is behind you. It is beside you. It is at your throat, very lightly. {npc} sheathes it and smiles. "Thank you," {he} says. "Now I know." (-6 health)

choices.text: Say you would rather not

effects.log: "I would rather not," you say. {npc} looks at you for a long time. Then {he} sheathes the sword. "That is the answer I was afraid of," {he} says. "The blade you choose not to eat." {He} goes away and never draws in anger again.

events.text: A general, {npc}, comes to your hill with maps. Invaders are coming over the northern border; {he} wants you to go up and eat their army's weapons in the passes, and {he} will give you anything.

choices.text: Go north and eat the invaders' weapons

effects.log: You go north to the passes and eat. A whole army, in the snow, in three nights. They go home with nothing. {npc} sends you a letter, which you cannot read, and has it read to you, and it is very long and very grateful.

choices.text: Ask {him} what {he} will do with the peace

effects.log: "And afterwards?" you ask. {npc} has not thought about afterwards. {He} thinks about it now, on your hill, for an hour. Then {he} goes north and makes a treaty without you, which nobody expected, least of all {him}.

events.text: A shaman, {npc}, comes up the hill with no bells and no charms, sits down on a stone near your head and starts to eat lunch. "My grandmother bound you with a charm once," {he} says. "The family says you were good company."

choices.text: Tell {him} about the grandmother

effects.log: You tell {npc} about the grandmother: the song, the lunches, the charm folded small. {He} listens with {his} mouth full and tears running down. "That is the old one," {he} says. "That is exactly right."

choices.text: Share the lunch

effects.log: You ask, very politely, for a little rice. {npc} gives you half. It is the best lunch you have had in a century.

events.text: A disciple, {npc}, has heard {his} dead master's voice come out of a hill, on the road, and has climbed up to find where it is coming from. {He} kneels by your ear. "Master," {he} says. "Is it you?"

choices.text: Answer in the master's voice

effects.log: You answer in the master's voice, because it is in you and wants to. It says three things only the master would know, and one thing the master never said in life: that {npc} was the best of them. {He} weeps and goes home changed.

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth gently

effects.log: "It is the sword," you say, in your own voice. "Only the sword remembers." {npc} sits by your ear until dark. "Then the sword remembers well," {he} says, and goes down.

events.text: A court official, {npc}, comes from the capital with an apology, of a kind: the court of the new kingdom regrets the Fire Hunts of the old one, and would like to know if you would consider guarding the palace against fire. {He} reads it out, very formally, from a scroll.

choices.text: Agree to watch over the palace

effects.log: "I will watch," you say. {npc} writes it down with great relief. You sleep on the hill above the palace every dry season after that. The court sends a bowl of rice every new year.

choices.text: Ask what the court will give the monks

effects.log: "And the monks?" you ask. {npc} has no answer in the scroll. {He} goes back to the capital with your question instead of your answer. It is debated for a year. A few temples get their land back.

events.text: A human, {npc}, as old and strong as you are in {his} own way, a master of the age who has outlived everyone, sits down on your foot. "I am tired," {he} says. "Are you? I thought we might stop together, one of these centuries."

choices.text: Say: not yet, but one day

effects.log: "Not yet," you say. "But one day." {npc} nods and stays a decade, sitting on your foot, and then goes on with {his} life, lighter. You will think of {him} when the day comes.

choices.text: Ask what stopping would look like for {him}

effects.log: "What would it look like?" you ask. {npc} thinks for a long time. "A garden," {he} says. "With no swords in it." You both laugh. Neither of you has ever planted anything.

events.text: An envoy from the Upper Realm, {npc}, stands on a cloud above your hill with a slate and a brush. "Heaven asks," {he} says, "what you intend to eat next. Heaven would like to be prepared."

choices.text: Say: fire, and fear

effects.log: "Fire," you say. "And fear, when I learn how." {npc} writes it down, and looks at it, and is visibly relieved. "Heaven can work with that," {he} says, and goes.

choices.text: Say: whatever is given

effects.log: "Whatever is given," you say. {npc} writes it down, and frowns at it, and underlines it. "That is either the safest answer or the most dangerous," {he} says. "Heaven will have to think." Heaven is still thinking.

events.text: A founder of bells, {npc}, comes up your hill with a burned hand and a question: the crossroads bell needs recasting again, and {his} guild has always told a story that you were part of the first one. Is it true?

choices.text: Tell {him} the story of the first pour

effects.log: You tell {npc} about the first pour, the river of bronze, the founder who did not breathe. {He} listens with {his} burned hand on your trunk. When {he} casts the new bell, {he} breathes for you, all the way through.

choices.text: Give {him} a little bronze for luck

effects.log: You give {npc} a little bronze from the bottom of you for the new bell, for luck. The bell is very good. It rings slightly flat, and the guild says that is how they know it is the real one.

events.text: A child, {npc}, who has climbed all the way to your head alone, sits on your eyebrow and asks you the question every child asks you sooner or later: "Why do you eat iron?"

choices.text: Say: because I was hungry, and it was there

effects.log: "Because I was hungry," you say, "and it was there." {npc} thinks about it seriously. "That is why I eat rice cakes," {he} says. You agree that you are much the same.

choices.text: Say: because somebody made me out of supper

effects.log: "Because somebody made me out of their supper," you say, "and supper is for eating." {npc} stares at you, then laughs so hard {he} nearly falls off your eyebrow.

events.text: A peak master, {npc}, has come to duel you, as {his} sect's elders demand, and stands at the foot of your hill with {his} sword drawn and {his} heart obviously not in it.

choices.text: Accept the duel

ok.log: You let {npc} cut at you for an hour, very well, and at the end take the sword out of {his} hand with your trunk and give it back. "Tell the elders you lost," you say. "To a hill." {He} goes home laughing.

fail.log: {npc} is better than {he} looked. A cut through the rust to the iron, and another. You are not hurt much. {He} goes home with a story the elders will like. (-6 health)

choices.text: Ask {him} if {he} wants to fight at all

effects.log: "Do you want to?" you ask. "No," says {npc}, and sits down. You talk about the elders all afternoon. {He} goes home and tells them a story that is mostly true.

events.text: A satirist, {npc}, the great-grandchild of the one who first called a greedy magistrate by your name, comes to apologise on the family's behalf, and also, it becomes clear, to ask you for a new poem.

choices.text: Give {him} a poem in a dead poet's voice

effects.log: You give {npc} a poem in the voice of one of the dead whose iron you carry. It is very good. {He} publishes it under {his} own name. You do not mind. The dead voice in you is delighted to be read again.

choices.text: Tell {him} the family owes you nothing

effects.log: "Your family owes me nothing," you say. "The magistrate was greedy." {npc} writes that down too. It becomes the last line of a very famous poem.
